claims.claim: Motor neurons can find their original targets even if they have been displaced to another segment of the spinal cord before axonal extension.
claims.source: MNs can find their original targets even if they have been displaced to another segment of the spinal cord before axonal extension, which indicates that most MNs are programmed with an intrinsic identity that encodes information on their targeting preference (Lance-Jones and Landmesser, 1980).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lance-Jones and Landmesser, 1980.

claims.claim: Motor neuron subtypes exhibit differential vulnerability in motor neuron-related degenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and spinal muscular atrophy.
claims.source: Moreover, MN subtypes exhibit differential vulnerability in MN-related degenerative diseases that cause progressive muscle weakness and paralysis, such as adult-onset amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and childhood spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), further support an intrinsic susceptibility to degeneration amongst MN subtypes.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of motor neuron subtypes in neurodegenerative diseases.

claims.claim: Spinal motor neurons are delineated according to the combinatorial actions of three homeodomain-containing transcription factors: Nkx2.2, Nkx6.1, and Irx3.
claims.source: Spinal MNs are delineated according to the combinatorial actions of three homeodomain-containing transcription factors (TFs) – Nkx2.2, Nkx6.1 and Irx3 – that confine the generation of motor neuron progenitors (pMNs) to the appropriate region of the neural tube (Balaskas et al., 2012; Briscoe et al., 2000)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Balaskas et al., 2012 and Briscoe et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Nkx2.2 and Irx3 initially ensure that motor neuron progenitors are induced in the ventral spinal cord.
claims.source: Nkx2.2 and Irx3 initially ensure that pMNs are induced in the ventral spinal cord.
claims.evidence: This is stated as part of the mechanism of motor neuron progenitor specification.

claims.claim: Nkx6.1 activity promotes the motor neuron progenitor-restricted induction of Olig2.
claims.source: Once pMNs have been defined, Nkx6.1 activity promotes the pMN-restricted induction of downstream factors, such as the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) factor Olig2 (Novitch et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Novitch et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Olig2 has a dual role in coordinating the acquisition of pan-neuronal properties and subtype characteristics of differentiating motor neurons.
claims.source: Olig2 has a dual role in coordinating the acquisition of pan-neuronal properties and subtype characteristics of differentiating MNs.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known function of Olig2 in motor neuron development.

claims.claim: Forced expression of Olig2 in the dorsal region is sufficient to repress Irx3.
claims.source: Forced expression of Olig2 in the dorsal region is sufficient to repress Irx3.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation about Olig2 function.

claims.claim: Progenitor domains are determined by a network of transcriptional repressors that repress all inappropriate and alternative cell fates to elicit a single definitive identity.
claims.source: Recent studies have further revealed the gene-regulatory network (GRN) of these progenitor TFs responsible for establishing cell identities in the developing spinal cord, with progenitor domains being determined by a network of transcriptional repressors that repress all inappropriate and alternative cell fates to elicit a single definitive identity (Figure 2A) (Kutejova et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kutejova et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Olig2 directly represses alternative interneuron domain transcription factors such as Pax6, Irx3, and Nkx2.2.
claims.source: For example, pMN-master regulator Olig2 directly represses alternative interneuron domain TFs such as Pax6, Irx3, and Nkx2.2.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an example of the cross-repressive mechanism in motor neuron progenitors.

claims.claim: In Olig2 mutants, Pax6 and Nkx2.2 are ectopically expanded into motor neuron progenitors.
claims.source: In Olig2 mutants, Pax6 and Nkx2.2 are ectopically expanded into pMNs, supporting the concept of cross-repressive TF-mediated GRN in the pMNs (Balaskas et al., 2012; Zhou and Anderson, 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Balaskas et al., 2012 and Zhou and Anderson, 2002.

claims.claim: In anamniotes, maintenance of motor neuron progenitors requires a motor neuron-specific Cyclin Dx (Ccndx).
claims.source: In anamniotes, maintenance of pMNs also requires an MN-specific Cyclin Dx (Ccndx).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a requirement for motor neuron progenitor maintenance in anamniotes.

claims.claim: Inhibition of Ccndx results in specific loss of differentiated motor neurons.
claims.source: Inhibition of Ccndx results in specific loss of differentiated MNs (Chen et al., 2007; Lien et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2007 and Lien et al., 2016.

claims.claim: In mouse embryos, spinal motor neurons acquire generic motor neuron identity after cell cycle exit at about embryonic day 9.5.
claims.source: In mouse embryos, spinal MNs acquire generic MN identity after cell cycle exit (i.e., at about embryonic day 9.5), and express a common set of TFs – Mnx1 (Hb9), Lhx3, Isl1 and Isl2 (Novitch et al., 2001; Thaler et al., 1999; Tsuchida et al., 1994)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Novitch et al., 2001; Thaler et al., 1999; and Tsuchida et al., 1994.

claims.claim: Generic spinal motor neuron identity is established by cooperative binding of the LIM complex comprising Isl1 and Lhx3 to motor neuron-specific enhancers.
claims.source: Generic spinal MN identity is established by cooperative binding of the LIM complex comprising Isl1 and Lhx3 to MN-specific enhancers, thereby inducing the expression of a battery of MN genes that induce functional hallmarks of MNs, while suppressing key interneuron genes.
claims.evidence: This is stated as the mechanism for establishing generic motor neuron identity.

claims.claim: The Isl1-Lhx3 complex amplifies its own expression through a potent autoregulatory feedback loop.
claims.source: Furthermore, the Isl1-Lhx3 complex amplifies its own expression through a potent autoregulatory feedback loop and simultaneously enhances the transcription of Lmo4 to promote MN differentiation and maturation (Erb et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Erb et al., 2017 and Lee et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Establishment of motor neuron subtype is mediated by mutually exclusive expression of Hox transcription factors programmed according to body segment along the rostrocaudal axis.
claims.source: As embryonic development progresses, MNs diversify to exhibit subtype identities. Establishment of MN subtype is mediated by mutually exclusive expression of Hox TFs, which is programmed according to body segment along the RC axis.
claims.evidence: This is stated as the mechanism for motor neuron subtype specification.

claims.claim: Segmental identity of motor neurons is defined by the mutually exclusive expression of Hox6, Hox9, and Hox10.
claims.source: For example, segmental identity of MNs is defined by the mutually exclusive expression of Hox6, Hox9 and Hox10 (Dasen et al., 2003; Lacombe et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dasen et al., 2003 and Lacombe et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Hoxc9 is required for the generation of thoracic motor neuron subtypes and is essential for organizing the motor neuron topographic map.
claims.source: In particular, a single Hox gene, Hoxc9, required for the generation of thoracic MN subtypes, is essential for organizing the MN topographic map, and acts as a key repressor of the forelimb-level Hox network (Jung et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jung et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Within the brachial segment hosting Hox6 expression, motor neurons are grouped into axial muscle-projecting motor neurons (Lhx3on, MMC) and forelimb-innervating motor neurons (Foxp1on, LMC).
claims.source: For instance, within the brachial segment hosting Hox6 expression, MNs are further grouped into axial muscle-projecting MNs (Lhx3on, MMC) and forelimb-innervating MNs (Foxp1on, LMC)(Dasen et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dasen et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Expression of Hox5 and Hox8 in Foxp1on LMC controls the rostral and caudal motor pool identity, which directs motor pools to innervate either proximal or distal muscles in the forelimb.
claims.source: Within Hoxc6on MNs, expression of another set of mutually exclusive Hox proteins, such as Hox5 and Hox8 in Foxp1on LMC, controls the rostral and caudal motor pool identity, which directs motor pools to either innervate proximal or distal muscles in the forelimb (Catela et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Catela et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Only Hoxc8 represses Hoxa5 unilaterally at protein level, despite a mutually exclusive Hoxa5-Hoxc8 sharp boundary being manifested within the Hoxc6on motor neurons.
claims.source: Although a mutually exclusive expressed Hoxa5-Hoxc8 sharp boundary is manifested within the Hoxc6on MNs, unlike progenitor-TFs that display mutual inhibitions, only Hoxc8 represses Hoxa5 unilaterally at protein level (Dasen et al., 2005; Li et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dasen et al., 2005 and Li et al., 2017.

claims.claim: LMC is further classified into divisional identities targeting flexor and extensor limb muscles.
claims.source: LMC is the most extensively studied motor column, and this motor column is further classified into divisional identities targeting flexor and extensor limb muscles (Kania and Jessell, 2003; Sockanathan and Jessell, 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kania and Jessell, 2003 and Sockanathan and Jessell, 1998.

claims.claim: Motor neurons labeled by retrograde labeling of each muscle group occupy distinct and stereotyped positions in the spinal cord.
claims.source: Further heterogeneity in spinal MNs can be revealed by retrograde labeling of each muscle group, with labeled MNs occupying distinct and stereotyped positions in the spinal cord (Hollyday, 1980a; Hollyday, 1980b; Landmesser, 1978a; Landmesser, 1978b; McHanwell and Biscoe, 1981; Romanes, 1964; Sürmeli et al., 2011; Vanderhorst and Holstege, 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using retrograde labeling.

claims.claim: Loss-of-function studies of Nkx6.1 and Nkx6.2 have resulted in target innervation and arborization defects in adductor and gracilis muscles.
claims.source: For example, Nkx6.1 and Nkx6.2 are expressed in subpopulations of MNs and loss-of-function studies of these proteins have resulted in target innervation and arborization defects in adductor and gracilis muscles (De Marco Garcia and Jessell, 2008; Ghosh and Kolodkin, 1998; Livet et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De Marco Garcia and Jessell, 2008; Ghosh and Kolodkin, 1998; and Livet et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Expression of the ETS-TF Etv4 (Pea3) in motor neurons innervating cutaneous maximus and latissimus dorsi muscles in the forelimb requires GDNF signal activation from the periphery.
claims.source: In addition, extrinsic cues are also indispensable for precisely defining MN subtype diversification and axon targeting. For example, expression of the ETS-TF Etv4 (Pea3) in MNs innervating cutaneous maximus and latissimus dorsi muscles in the forelimb requires GDNF signal activation from the periphery (Haase et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haase et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Cpne4/Fign markers and evasion of non-canonical retinoic acid signaling label the motor neuron subtype innervating digit muscles.
claims.source: Recently, Jessell and colleagues revealed that Cpne4/Fign markers and evasion of non-canonical retinoic acid signaling label the MN subtype innervating digit muscles, providing insights into the emergence of a divergent molecular program during evolution (Mendelsohn et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mendelsohn et al., 2017.

claims.claim: 60 motor pools are thought to exist in either the brachial or lumbar LMC motor neurons innervating mouse limb muscles.
claims.source: Even though 60 motor pools are thought to exist in either the brachial or lumbar LMC-MNs innervating mouse limb muscles, a complete subtype-specific gene profile for each motor pool is still lacking, not to mention for the other less well-profiled motor columns (D'Elia and Dasen, 2018; Fetcho, 1987)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to D'Elia and Dasen, 2018 and Fetcho, 1987.

claims.claim: More than one-third of the genes in the human genome might be regulated by microRNAs.
claims.source: It has been proposed that more than one-third of the genes in the human genome might be regulated by miRNAs (Lewis et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lewis et al., 2005.

claims.claim: miR-17–3p is required to silence transient Olig2 expression in p2 progenitors.
claims.source: By disrupting miRNA biogenesis during simulated DV patterning of differentiating ES cells both in cellulo and in vivo, it was revealed that miR-17–3p, a member of the miR-17 ~92 cluster, is required to silence transient Olig2 expression in p2 progenitors (Chen et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Specific timing of miR-196 expression is required for proper motor neuron differentiation, which is mediated by downregulation of Hoxb8.
claims.source: In the developing spinal cord of chick embryos, specific timing of miR-196 expression is required for proper MN differentiation, which is mediated by downregulation of Hoxb8.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from studies in chick embryos.

claims.claim: Failure to clear Hoxb8 in a spatial and temporal manner abolishes motor neuron generation.
claims.source: Failure to clear Hoxb8 in a spatial and temporal manner abolishes MN generation (Asli and Kessel, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Asli and Kessel, 2010.

claims.claim: In conditional neural Dicer mutants, Hoxa5 protein is precociously expressed at progenitors and the Hox5/8 boundary is expanded caudally.
claims.source: In conditional neural Dicer mutants (Sox1-Cre; Dicerfloxed, Dicer NeuralΔ ) in which all mature miRNA production is abrogated in the CNS, Hoxa5 protein is precociously expressed at progenitors and the Hox5/8 boundary is expanded caudally, both in cellulo and in vivo (Figure 3B) (Li et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2017 and reference to Figure 3B.

claims.claim: miR-27 is a major regulator coordinating the temporal delay and spatial boundary of Hox protein expression.
claims.source: Using in silico simulation, two feed-forward Hox-miRNA loops have been uncovered that account for the precocious and noisy Hoxa5 expression, as well as the ill-defined boundary phenotype of Dicer mutants. In this scenario, miR-27 appears to be a major regulator coordinating the temporal delay and spatial boundary of Hox protein expression.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from in silico simulation studies.

claims.claim: Expression of miR-218 is directly upregulated by the Isl1-Lhx3 complex to drive motor neuron fate.
claims.source: In the developing spinal cord, expression of miR-218 is directly upregulated by the Isl1-Lhx3 complex to drive MN fate (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a mechanism of miR-218 regulation in motor neuron development.

claims.claim: Loss of miR-218 function leads to impaired generation of generic motor neurons.
claims.source: Loss of miR-218 function leads to impaired generation of generic MNs, suggesting that this miRNA plays a crucial role in MN differentiation (Amin et al., 2015; Thiebes et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amin et al., 2015 and Thiebes et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Mutant mice lacking miR-218 die neonatally and exhibit neuromuscular junction defects, motor neuron hyperexcitability, and progressive motor neuron degeneration.
claims.source: Furthermore, mutant mice lacking miR-218 die neonatally and exhibit neuromuscular junction defects, MN hyperexcitability, and progressive MN degeneration, recapitulating traits of motor neuron disease (Amin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amin et al., 2015.

claims.claim: miR-218 represses an array of transcripts in the alternative neighboring interneuron genes to maintain postmitotic motor neuron cell fate and robust neuromuscular functions.
claims.source: However, miR-218 does not seem to exert its functions by targeting a few specific genes. Instead, it appears to repress an array of transcripts in the alternative neighboring interneuron genes to maintain postmitotic MN cell fate and robust neuromuscular functions (Amin et al., 2015; Thiebes et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amin et al., 2015 and Thiebes et al., 2015.

claims.claim: miR-218 is encoded by an intron of the extracellular matrix Slit2 and Slit3 genes.
claims.source: Interestingly, miR-218 is encoded by an intron of the extracellular matrix Slit2 and Slit3 genes and it inhibits expression of neural cell adhesion molecules Robo1 and Robo2 and multiple components of the heparan sulfate biosynthetic pathway responsible for normal vascularization of the retina (Small et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Small et al., 2010.

claims.claim: miR-9 is transiently expressed in Foxp1on LMC regions.
claims.source: For instance, miR-9 is transiently expressed in Foxp1on LMC regions.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation about miR-9 expression pattern.

claims.claim: Overexpression or knockdown of miR-9 alters motor neuron subtypes, switches columnar identities, and changes axonal innervations in developing chick spinal cords.
claims.source: Overexpression or knockdown of miR-9 alters MN subtypes, switches columnar identities, and changes axonal innervations in developing chick spinal cords.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding in chick spinal cords.

claims.claim: miR-9 modifies spinal columnar organization by specifically regulating Foxp1 protein levels.
claims.source: miR-9 modifies spinal columnar organization by specifically regulating Foxp1 protein levels, which in turn determine distinct MN subtypes (Otaegi et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Otaegi et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Deletion of Dicer from all motor neurons using Olig2-Cre revealed a preferential loss of many limb- and sympathetic ganglia-innervating spinal motor neurons.
claims.source: Additionally, deletion of the enzyme Dicer from all MNs using Olig2-Cre (Dicer MNΔ ) revealed a preferential loss of many limb- and sympathetic ganglia-innervating spinal MNs (Chen and Wichterle, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen and Wichterle, 2012.

claims.claim: Disruption of Dicer in motor neurons led to defects in motor pool identity specification.
claims.source: Furthermore, this disruption also led to defects in motor pool identity specification, yet the miRNA candidates to maintain motor pool identity have yet to be unveiled (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from Dicer deletion studies.

claims.claim: The miR-17~92 cluster is highly enriched in LMC motor neurons.
claims.source: Subsequent study uncovered that the miR-17 ~92 cluster is highly enriched in LMC-MNs.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from subsequent studies.

claims.claim: Conditional motor neuron miR-17~92 deletion resulted in selective cell death of LMC motor neurons.
claims.source: Furthermore, conditional MN miR-17 ~92 deletion (mi-17 ~92 MNΔ ) resulted in selective cell death of LMC-MNs.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claims.claim: miR-17~92 not only suppresses PTEN expression, but also independently attenuates accumulation of nuclear PTEN.
claims.source: Mechanistically, mir-17 ~92 not only suppresses PTEN expression, but also independently attenuates accumulation of nuclear PTEN, with this latter being a more potent apoptosis stimulator (Tung et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tung et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Reduced miR-17~92 is accompanied by elevated nuclear PTEN in the spinal motor neurons of presymptomatic SOD1G93A mice.
claims.source: Tellingly, reduced miR-17 ~92 is accompanied by elevated nuclear PTEN in the spinal MNs of presymptomatic SOD1G93A mice, that is the most common mouse strain used as an ALS disease model.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation in the ALS mouse model.

claims.claim: Overexpression of miR-17~92 significantly rescues human SOD1+/L144F motor neurons.
claims.source: Furthermore, overexpression of miR-17 ~92 significantly rescues human SOD1+/L144F MNs, and intrathecal delivery of scAAV9 [self-complementary adeno-associated viral serotype 9]-miR-17 ~ 92 improves motor deficits and survival in SOD1G93A mice (Tung et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tung et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Intrathecal delivery of scAAV9-miR-17~92 improves motor deficits and survival in SOD1G93A mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, overexpression of miR-17 ~92 significantly rescues human SOD1+/L144F MNs, and intrathecal delivery of scAAV9 [self-complementary adeno-associated viral serotype 9]-miR-17 ~ 92 improves motor deficits and survival in SOD1G93A mice (Tung et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tung et al., 2019.

claims.claim: SMA is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease characterized by devastating muscular atrophy attributable to progressive spinal motor neuron degeneration.
claims.source: SMA is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease characterized by devastating muscular atrophy attributable to progressive spinal MN degeneration.
claims.evidence: This is a standard definition of SMA provided in the text.

claims.claim: SMA has an estimated worldwide incidence of one in 6,000 to 10,000 newborns.
claims.source: Although SMA is a relatively rare disease, with an estimated worldwide incidence of one in 6,000 ~ 10,000 newborns, it is notable that SMA is the second most common autosomal recessive disease after cystic fibrosis and is the most common monogenic defect leading to infant mortality (Lunn and Wang, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lunn and Wang, 2008.

claims.claim: SMA is the second most common autosomal recessive disease after cystic fibrosis.
claims.source: Although SMA is a relatively rare disease, with an estimated worldwide incidence of one in 6,000 ~ 10,000 newborns, it is notable that SMA is the second most common autosomal recessive disease after cystic fibrosis and is the most common monogenic defect leading to infant mortality (Lunn and Wang, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lunn and Wang, 2008.

claims.claim: SMA is the most common monogenic defect leading to infant mortality.
claims.source: Although SMA is a relatively rare disease, with an estimated worldwide incidence of one in 6,000 ~ 10,000 newborns, it is notable that SMA is the second most common autosomal recessive disease after cystic fibrosis and is the most common monogenic defect leading to infant mortality (Lunn and Wang, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lunn and Wang, 2008.

claims.claim: SMA is caused by reduced levels of the 38 kDa Survival Motor Neuron (SMN) protein due to deletion or mutation of the Survival of Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1) gene.
claims.source: SMA is caused by reduced levels of the 38 kDa Survival Motor Neuron (SMN) protein due to deletion or mutation of the Survival of Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1) gene.
claims.evidence: This is stated as the genetic cause of SMA.

claims.claim: SMN protein is encoded by two genes in humans: SMN1 and highly homologous SMN2, which differ by one nucleotide (C→T) in exon 7.
claims.source: In humans, SMN protein is actually encoded by two genes: SMN1 and highly homologous SMN2, which essentially differs by one nucleotide (C→T) in exon 7.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a fact about human SMN genes.

claims.claim: The C→T nucleotide difference in exon 7 of SMN2 results in preferential exclusion of exon seven from most SMN2 transcripts.
claims.source: This critical difference results in preferential exclusion of exon seven from most SMN2 transcripts, termed SMN△7.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the nucleotide difference.

claims.claim: SMN2 generates approximately 10% of full-length SMN mRNAs and their product-functional SMN proteins.
claims.source: As a consequence, SMN2 generates ~10% of full-length (FL) SMN mRNAs and their product-functional SMN proteins (Burghes and Beattie, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Burghes and Beattie, 2009.

claims.claim: The full-length SMN2 transcript copy number may determine phenotypic severity in SMA patients.
claims.source: As these FL-SMN2 transcripts can partially compensate for loss of SMN1, it is reasoned that the FL-SMN2 transcript copy number may determine phenotypic severity in SMA patients.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a reasoning about SMA phenotypic severity.

claims.claim: Additional modifiers might be involved in modulating SMA clinical severity beyond SMN2 copy number.
claims.source: However, recent studies have indicated that additional modifiers might also be involved in modulating SMA clinical severity (Crawford et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crawford et al., 2012.

claims.claim: SMN is ubiquitously expressed in almost all kinds of somatic cells, with a distribution in both the cytoplasm and nucleus.
claims.source: SMN is ubiquitously expressed in almost all kinds of somatic cells, with a distribution in both the cytoplasm and nucleus (Burghes and Beattie, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Burghes and Beattie, 2009.

claims.claim: The most appreciated canonical role of SMN is to serve as an essential ribonucleoprotein for mRNA splicing.
claims.source: Notably, the most appreciated canonical role of SMN is to serve as an essential ribonucleoprotein (RNP) for mRNA splicing.
claims.evidence: This is stated as the canonical role of SMN.

claims.claim: SMN protein is embedded in a complex with seven Gemins and UNRIP that loads Sm protein onto nascent U-snRNAs upon their export to the cytoplasm.
claims.source: SMN protein is embedded in a complex with seven Gemins and UNR-interacting protein (UNRIP) that loads Sm protein onto nascent uridine-rich noncoding RNAs (U-snRNAs) upon their export to the cytoplasm, thereby creating small nuclear RNPs (snRNPs) that form spliceosomes in the nucleus (Burghes and Beattie, 2009; Dostie et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burghes and Beattie, 2009 and Dostie et al., 2003.

claims.claim: The SMN complex has a role in assisting arginine methylation of some splicing-related proteins involved in pre-mRNA splicing.
claims.source: In addition to facilitating snRNP assembly, the SMN complex has a role in assisting arginine methylation of some splicing-related proteins that are involved in pre-mRNA splicing (Meister and Fischer, 2002; Pellizzoni et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Meister and Fischer, 2002 and Pellizzoni et al., 2002.

claims.claim: There is a direct correlation between the ability to assemble snRNPs and SMA phenotypes in animal models.
claims.source: Studies on SMA animal models have also revealed a direct correlation between the ability to assemble snRNPs and SMA phenotypes, and delivery of mature snRNPs even without the SMN component is sufficient to rescue SMA phenotypes (Gabanella et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2005; Workman et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gabanella et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2005; and Workman et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Delivery of mature snRNPs without the SMN component is sufficient to rescue SMA phenotypes.
claims.source: Studies on SMA animal models have also revealed a direct correlation between the ability to assemble snRNPs and SMA phenotypes, and delivery of mature snRNPs even without the SMN component is sufficient to rescue SMA phenotypes (Gabanella et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2005; Workman et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gabanella et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2005; and Workman et al., 2009.

claims.claim: SMN protein levels might affect splicing of SMN pre-mRNA to include exon seven through an autoregulatory loop.
claims.source: This outcome implies that SMN protein levels might affect splicing of SMN pre-mRNA to include exon seven through an autoregulatory loop, thereby influencing a general process of snRNP biogenesis (Jodelka et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jodelka et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Assembly of SMN protein is involved in DNA repair and protein/mRNA transportation along motor neuron axons.
claims.source: For example, assembly of SMN protein is also involved in a number of essential cellular pathways, including DNA repair and protein/mRNA transportation along MN axons (Donlin-Asp et al., 2016; Fallini et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Donlin-Asp et al., 2016; Fallini et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2015; and Tu et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Deletion of the miRNA biogenesis enzyme Dicer in motor neurons results in motor neuron degeneration that mimics certain hallmarks of SMA and ALS.
claims.source: Deletion of the miRNA biogenesis enzyme Dicer in MNs either using Olig2-Cre or ChAT-Cre results in MN degeneration that mimics certain hallmarks of SMA and ALS (Chen and Wichterle, 2012; Haramati et al., 2010; Tung et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen and Wichterle, 2012; Haramati et al., 2010; and Tung et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Gemin3 and Gemin4 of the SMN complex can assemble with a number of miRNAs to form a miRNA-binding RNP (miRNP).
claims.source: For example, Gemin3 and Gemin4 of the SMN complex can assemble with a number of miRNAs to form a miRNA-binding RNP (miRNP) (Dostie et al., 2003; Mourelatos et al., 2002)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dostie et al., 2003 and Mourelatos et al., 2002.

claims.claim: The miRNP complex can bind to Argonaute 2 (AGO2) that functions as a core protein in the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) mediating miRNA biogenesis and mRNA posttranscriptional regulation.
claims.source: This miRNP complex can further bind to Argonaute 2 (AGO2) that functions as a core protein in the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) mediating miRNA biogenesis as well as mRNA posttranscriptional regulation (Cauchi, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cauchi, 2010.

claims.claim: SMN interacts with miRNA biogenesis proteins including FMRP, KSRP, and FUS/TLS.
claims.source: Interestingly, in addition to the role of SMN in RNA processing, recent studies have uncovered unexpected interactions of SMN with miRNA biogenesis proteins including fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP), KH‐type splicing regulatory protein (KSRP) and fused in sarcoma/translocated in liposarcoma (FUS/TLS) (Piazzon et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2015; Tadesse et al., 2008; Yamazaki et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Piazzon et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2015; Tadesse et al., 2008; and Yamazaki et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Deficiency of SMN may alter motor neuron-specific miRNAs or miRNPs, resulting in motor neuron death.
claims.source: Thus, SMN is engaged in miRNA–RBP complexes and likely regulates miRNA biogenesis and metabolism. Deficiency of SMN may alter MN-specific miRNAs or miRNPs, resulting in MN death (Cauchi, 2010; Nelson et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cauchi, 2010 and Nelson et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Reduced SMN activity specifically affects miR-2 expression, which causes motor neurons to produce more m2R, a receptor for acetylcholine.
claims.source: By using both mouse and nematode models of SMA, O' Hern et al. showed that reduced SMN activity specifically affects miR-2 expression, which in turn causes MNs to produce more m2R, a receptor for acetylcholine (O'Hern et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to O'Hern et al., 2017.

claims.claim: SMN protein levels in astrocytes affect both directly and indirectly altered expression levels of miR-146a.
claims.source: Interestingly, it was recently shown that SMN protein levels in astrocytes affect both directly and indirectly altered expression levels of miR-146a (Sison et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sison et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Increased levels of miR-146a in the SMNΔ7 mouse spinal cord are linked to astrocyte-mediated SMA pathology.
claims.source: The proposed mechanism for that astrocyte-mediated SMA pathology was linked to increased levels of miR-146a in the SMNΔ7 mouse spinal cord.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism for SMA pathology.

claims.claim: Treating iPSC-derived motor neurons with synthesized miR-146a molecules was sufficient to induce significant motor neuron loss.
claims.source: Although the precise targets of miR-146a have not yet been identified, treating iPSC-derived MNs with synthesized miR-146a molecules was sufficient to induce significant MN loss.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Finkel et al., 2017 and Mendell et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Quantification of SMN mRNA or protein levels does not necessarily correlate with disease severity and may not reliably reflect disease progression in SMA.
claims.source: Quantification of SMN mRNA or protein levels has served as the most commonly used molecular biomarker of SMA, but it does not necessarily correlate with disease severity and may not reliably reflect disease progression (Sumner et al., 2006; Wadman et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sumner et al., 2006 and Wadman et al., 2016.

claims.claim: MiRNAs are clinically detectable in many biofluids such as cerebrospinal fluid, serum/plasma, saliva, and urine using noninvasive methods.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Viswambharan et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved the first drug utilizing RNA interference for adult clinical treatment of hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis.

results.result: Spinal motor neurons are well-characterized for studying neuronal identity establishment and selective vulnerability in neurodegenerative diseases. Motor neurons exhibit intrinsic identity encoding target preference and differential vulnerability in diseases like ALS and SMA.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 establish the rationale for studying motor neurons. C1 and C4 are general knowledge statements about motor neuron utility and disease vulnerability. C3 is supported by a classic citation (Lance-Jones and Landmesser, 1980) demonstrating intrinsic motor neuron identity. These claims provide appropriate background context.

results.result: Motor neuron progenitor specification is controlled by combinatorial actions of transcription factors Nkx2.2, Nkx6.1, Irx3, and Olig2 through cross-repressive gene regulatory networks. Olig2 directly represses alternative interneuron domain factors, and loss of Olig2 results in ectopic expansion of Pax6 and Nkx2.2 into motor neuron progenitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C12 describe the well-established transcriptional network controlling motor neuron progenitor specification. Multiple citations support the cross-repressive mechanisms (Balaskas et al., 2012; Briscoe et al., 2000; Novitch et al., 2001; Kutejova et al., 2016; Zhou and Anderson, 2002). The genetic evidence from Olig2 mutants (C12) provides experimental validation of the proposed network.

results.result: In anamniotes, motor neuron progenitor maintenance requires motor neuron-specific Cyclin Dx (Ccndx), and inhibition of Ccndx results in specific loss of differentiated motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14 describe a specific requirement for Ccndx in anamniotes, supported by citations to Chen et al., 2007 and Lien et al., 2016. However, the text notes this mechanism may not apply to amniotes, limiting the generalizability of this finding.

results.result: Generic motor neuron identity is established after cell cycle exit through cooperative binding of the Isl1-Lhx3 LIM complex to motor neuron-specific enhancers, which induces motor neuron genes while suppressing interneuron genes and amplifies its own expression through autoregulatory feedback.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 describe the well-characterized mechanism of generic motor neuron specification. Multiple citations support the role of the Isl1-Lhx3 complex (Novitch et al., 2001; Thaler et al., 1999; Tsuchida et al., 1994; Erb et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2012). This represents established knowledge in the field.

results.result: Motor neuron subtype diversification is mediated by mutually exclusive expression of Hox transcription factors along the rostrocaudal axis. Hox6, Hox9, and Hox10 define segmental identity, while Hoxc9 is essential for thoracic motor neuron subtypes. Within segments, Hox5 and Hox8 control motor pool identity, though Hoxc8 represses Hoxa5 unilaterally rather than through mutual inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 describe the Hox-mediated motor neuron subtype specification, supported by multiple citations (Dasen et al., 2003, 2005, 2008; Lacombe et al., 2013; Jung et al., 2010; Catela et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017). The unilateral repression by Hoxc8 (C23) is an important mechanistic detail distinguishing this from progenitor-level cross-repression.

results.result: Motor neurons exhibit further diversification into motor pools with distinct muscle targets. LMC is classified into divisional identities, and retrograde labeling reveals stereotyped positions. Loss-of-function studies show roles for Nkx6.1/6.2, Etv4, and Cpne4/Fign markers in target innervation, though complete motor pool gene profiles remain incomplete.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29 describe motor pool diversification with appropriate citations. C29 acknowledges that despite ~60 motor pools existing, complete subtype-specific gene profiles are lacking, which is an honest assessment of the field's current limitations.

results.result: More than one-third of human genes may be regulated by microRNAs. miR-17-3p is required to silence transient Olig2 expression in p2 progenitors during dorsoventral patterning.
results.evaluation: Claim C30 provides general context about miRNA prevalence (Lewis et al., 2005). C31 describes a specific finding about miR-17-3p function in progenitor patterning (Chen et al., 2011), supported by both in cellulo and in vivo experiments. This represents a concrete example of miRNA function in neural patterning.

results.result: miR-196 and miR-27 regulate Hox protein expression timing and spatial boundaries. miR-196 downregulates Hoxb8 for proper motor neuron differentiation, while miR-27 coordinates temporal delay and spatial boundaries of Hoxa5 expression. In Dicer mutants, Hoxa5 is precociously expressed and the Hox5/8 boundary is expanded.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 describe miRNA regulation of Hox expression. C32-C33 are supported by chick embryo studies (Asli and Kessel, 2010). C34-C35 describe findings from Dicer mutants (Li et al., 2017) and in silico simulations identifying miR-27 as a key regulator. The combination of genetic and computational evidence supports these claims.

results.result: miR-218 is directly upregulated by the Isl1-Lhx3 complex and is crucial for motor neuron differentiation. Loss of miR-218 leads to impaired motor neuron generation, neonatal lethality, neuromuscular junction defects, and motor neuron degeneration. miR-218 functions by repressing multiple interneuron transcripts rather than specific targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 describe miR-218 function in motor neurons, supported by citations to Amin et al., 2015 and Thiebes et al., 2015. The knockout phenotype (C38) provides strong genetic evidence. C39 describes the mechanism as broad transcript repression rather than specific targeting, and C40 notes the genomic location within Slit genes.

results.result: miR-9 is transiently expressed in Foxp1-positive LMC regions and modifies spinal columnar organization by regulating Foxp1 protein levels. Overexpression or knockdown of miR-9 alters motor neuron subtypes and axonal innervations in chick spinal cords.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 describe miR-9 function in motor neuron subtype specification. The experimental manipulations in chick (C42) and the mechanistic link to Foxp1 regulation (C43, Otaegi et al., 2011) provide evidence for this role. However, the text later notes that mouse knockout validation would be prudent.

results.result: Deletion of Dicer from motor neurons reveals preferential loss of limb-innervating motor neurons and defects in motor pool identity. The miR-17~92 cluster is highly enriched in LMC motor neurons, and its deletion causes selective LMC motor neuron death through regulation of PTEN expression and nuclear localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 describe findings from Dicer and miR-17~92 deletion studies (Chen and Wichterle, 2012; Tung et al., 2015). The genetic evidence is strong, showing selective effects on LMC motor neurons. C48 provides mechanistic insight into PTEN regulation. C45 acknowledges that specific miRNAs for motor pool identity remain unidentified.

results.result: Reduced miR-17~92 and elevated nuclear PTEN are observed in presymptomatic SOD1G93A ALS mice. Overexpression of miR-17~92 rescues human SOD1+/L144F motor neurons, and intrathecal delivery of scAAV9-miR-17~92 improves motor deficits and survival in SOD1G93A mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 link miR-17~92 to ALS pathology and demonstrate therapeutic potential (Tung et al., 2019). The progression from observational findings (C49) to rescue experiments in human iPSC-derived motor neurons (C50) to in vivo therapeutic delivery (C51) provides strong evidence for the role of miR-17~92 in ALS.

results.result: SMA is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease caused by reduced SMN protein due to SMN1 deletion/mutation. SMN2, differing by one nucleotide in exon 7, produces ~10% full-length SMN. SMN2 copy number may determine phenotypic severity, though additional modifiers are involved.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C61 provide standard background on SMA genetics and epidemiology, supported by citations (Lunn and Wang, 2008; Burghes and Beattie, 2009; Crawford et al., 2012). C60 appropriately uses cautious language ('may determine') and C61 acknowledges additional modifiers, showing appropriate scientific nuance.

results.result: SMN is ubiquitously expressed and functions as an essential ribonucleoprotein in mRNA splicing. The SMN complex loads Sm proteins onto U-snRNAs to create snRNPs. Delivery of mature snRNPs without SMN is sufficient to rescue SMA phenotypes in animal models. SMN also functions in DNA repair and axonal transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C69 describe SMN's canonical and non-canonical functions, well-supported by multiple citations (Burghes and Beattie, 2009; Dostie et al., 2003; Meister and Fischer, 2002; Pellizzoni et al., 2002; Gabanella et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2005; Workman et al., 2009; Jodelka et al., 2010; Donlin-Asp et al., 2016; Fallini et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2017). The rescue experiments (C67) provide strong evidence for the importance of snRNP assembly.

results.result: Deletion of Dicer in motor neurons mimics SMA/ALS hallmarks. SMN complex components Gemin3/4 assemble with miRNAs to form miRNPs that bind AGO2 in RISC. SMN interacts with miRNA biogenesis proteins including FMRP, KSRP, and FUS/TLS. SMN deficiency may alter motor neuron-specific miRNAs, resulting in motor neuron death.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are supported by citations describing Dicer deletion phenotypes and SMN-miRNA pathway interactions (Chen and Wichterle, 2012; Haramati et al., 2010; Tung et al., 2019; Dostie et al., 2003; Mourelatos et al., 2002; Cauchi, 2010; Piazzon et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2015; Tadesse et al., 2008; Yamazaki et al., 2012). However, C74 is speculative ('may alter'), and the text notes SMN doesn't directly bind miRNP, leaving the functional significance uncertain.

results.result: Reduced SMN activity affects miR-2 expression, causing increased m2R acetylcholine receptor production in motor neurons. SMN levels in astrocytes affect miR-146a expression, and increased miR-146a in SMA mouse spinal cord is linked to astrocyte-mediated pathology. Treating iPSC-derived motor neurons with miR-146a induces motor neuron loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 describe specific miRNA dysregulation in SMA models (O'Hern et al., 2017; Sison et al., 2017). C75 provides mechanistic insight into neuromuscular junction dysfunction. C76-C78 describe non-cell-autonomous effects through astrocytes. However, C77 is described as a 'proposed mechanism' and C78 notes targets are unidentified, indicating incomplete mechanistic understanding.

results.result: Two SMA treatment trials using antisense oligonucleotides (Nusinersen) or virus-mediated gene therapy (scAAV9-SMN1) exhibited promising outcomes. These approaches aim to increase SMN protein production through different mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 describe current SMA therapies supported by citations to clinical trials (Finkel et al., 2017; Mendell et al., 2017). These represent established therapeutic approaches, though the text later discusses challenges including cost, delivery, and variable patient responses.

results.result: SMN mRNA/protein levels do not necessarily correlate with disease severity or progression. miRNAs are detectable in biofluids using noninvasive methods. miR-9, miR-132, miR-206, miR-183, and miR-375 have been proposed as potential SMA biomarkers.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is supported by citations showing limitations of SMN as a biomarker (Sumner et al., 2006; Wadman et al., 2016). C83 describes the general utility of miRNAs as biomarkers (Viswambharan et al., 2017). However, C84 states these miRNAs have been 'proposed' as biomarkers without validation data, and the text notes it remains to be tested if they indicate treatment efficacy.

results.result: A phase 3 antisense oligonucleotide trial for severe infantile SMA revealed distinct patient responses. The time between first symptoms and treatment initiation was the only identified factor influencing response.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 describe findings from a clinical trial (Finkel et al., 2017). The text notes this factor doesn't satisfactorily explain outcome variation, highlighting the need for better biomarkers to stratify patients.

results.result: Reintroduction of miR-23a via scAAV9 into SMA mice increased motor neuron size, reduced neuromuscular junction pathology, and extended survival. Only 16 miRNAs showed >2-fold reduced expression in SMA motor neurons compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 describe recent findings from Kaifer et al., 2019. C87 provides therapeutic proof-of-concept, though mechanistic details are incomplete. C88 suggests only a subset of miRNAs may be causative in SMA, which is an important finding for targeting therapeutic interventions.

results.result: Approximately 5 miRNAs are highly or specifically expressed in motor neurons, but only two mouse knockout lines (miR-17~92MNΔ and miR-218 double knockout) have been characterized in detail.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 provide an honest assessment of the current state of the field. The text acknowledges this limitation and suggests future directions using CRISPR-Cas9 technology to overcome challenges with miRNA paralogs.

results.result: The U.S. FDA approved the first RNA interference drug for treating hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 states a factual regulatory milestone, providing context for the potential of RNA-based therapeutics. This is used to frame the discussion of challenges remaining for miRNA-based therapies in neurodegenerative diseases.

results.result: Motor neurons are organized into distinct columns along the rostrocaudal axis: limb-innervating LMC at brachial/lumbar levels, preganglionic and hypaxial neurons at thoracic levels, and medial motor neurons at all levels projecting to epaxial muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 describe the basic anatomical organization of motor neuron columns, illustrated in Figure 1. This represents well-established neuroanatomical knowledge providing essential context for understanding motor neuron diversity.

results.result: Sonic hedgehog gradients from the notochord/floor plate and BMP/TGFβ from the roof plate mediate dorsoventral patterning by repressing class I and inducing class II homeodomain proteins. Retinoic acid from paraxial mesoderm induces class I proteins. Shh signaling defines five progenitor domains giving rise to interneurons and motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 describe the fundamental morphogen-based patterning of the neural tube, illustrated in Figure 2A. This represents well-established developmental biology knowledge essential for understanding motor neuron specification.

results.result: FGF signals maintain a caudal progenitor zone during axis extension, and RA-mediated downregulation of FGF is required for neuronal patterning at rostral levels. The RA/FGF gradient elicits Hox gene expression along the rostrocaudal axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 describe rostrocaudal patterning mechanisms illustrated in Figure 2C. This represents established knowledge about how opposing morphogen gradients pattern the developing spinal cord along the anterior-posterior axis.
